 Path('tmp').rmdir()

strengths: The practical objective is valuable: sharing one model across ten heterogeneous facial analysis tasks could simplify deployment and reduce duplicated computation.

The reported results demonstrate competitive performance across several tasks, including 3.52 MAE on BIWI, 3.05 full-set NME on 300W, and 91.83% attribute accuracy on CelebA. Such breadth is useful even when specialized models remain stronger.

Component and backbone ablations provide supporting evidence, and cross-dataset evaluation extends beyond qualitative examples. In particular, 300VW Category C improves from STARLoss's 8.42 NME to 6.75.

The manuscript identifies dataset sources, describes licensing procedures, and includes demographic evaluation. These are constructive elements, although the conclusions drawn from the demographic results require qualification.
weaknesses: A material numerical inconsistency affects the headline parsing result. In Table 3, FaceXFormer's ten class scores average to 91.01, not 92.01. The margin over Faceptor therefore becomes 0.12 rather than 1.12 points. The corrected result remains competitive, but the manuscript substantially overstates its improvement.

Architectural originality is insufficiently established. Task-token unification already appears in QFace and Faceptor, while FaceX's token self-attention and bidirectional token/image cross-attention closely follow SAM's two-way decoder. SAM is cited as background, but the manuscript does not explain the architectural distinction supporting its central novelty claim.

The simultaneous-inference claim needs stronger verification. Appendices F.2 and F.7 describe five-keypoint alignment for landmarks and recognition, whereas F.3 uses loose crops for pose. Section 4.2 also mentions three additional epochs for unspecified tasks. It remains unclear whether all reported results correspond to one final checkpoint and whether one common preprocessing pipeline preserves those results.

Important reproduction details are missing or inconsistent. The loss weights are unspecified, and reconciliation of different demographic label spaces is unclear. Appendix F.5 introduces MORPH-II training/evaluation and FFHQ testing, whereas the main protocol lists different datasets and reports UTKFace age results. These discrepancies affect interpretation of the training data and benchmark comparisons.

Experimental coverage does not fully establish the claimed benefits of ten-task learning. Race classification has no quantitative evaluation. There are no matched-backbone, matched-data single-task or task-addition experiments to separate beneficial task transfer from architectural and training-data differences. The cross-dataset evidence supports only a subset of the broad robustness claims.

The efficiency comparison lacks a sufficiently specified inference setup, including timing hardware, batch size, and preprocessing costs. Different backbones, resolutions, and task sets also prevent attributing the reported speed advantage specifically to bidirectional attention. A controlled decoder-depth comparison would better support the two-layer efficiency argument.

The 'minimal bias' conclusion exceeds Table 8's evidence. FaceXFormer's age accuracy gap of 0.50 is larger than CLIP's absolute gap of 0.30 and FaRL's 0.35. Aggregating six racial categories can conceal subgroup disparities, and no ablation supports attributing fairness to race co-training. The proposed surveillance and automatic-annotation applications also deserve discussion of privacy, demographic-label limitations, and error propagation.
